title: Extortionate restrictive covenants, children's religious freedom, and harmful pet breeding
label: 10 November 2026 · Backbench debate proposals
summary: The Backbench Business Committee considered three proposed Westminster Hall debates: (1) homeowners targeted by a firm called Asset Invest buying restrictive covenants and demanding large payments; (2) protecting the next generation’s freedom of religion or belief overseas; and (3) the harms of breeding dogs and cats with exaggerated features. MPs seeking the debates explained the problems, gave concrete examples and asked for Government engagement; the Chair asked for additional Government speakers for the first application and the Clerks will follow up on logistics and Departments responsible.

chapters.title: Homeowners targeted over restrictive covenants
chapters.takeaway: A company called Asset Invest has been buying restrictive covenants and demanding large payments from homeowners when they try to sell, and MPs want a Westminster Hall debate to raise the issue nationally and feed into leasehold reform.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Marie, please present your case for a Westminster Hall debate on protection for homeowners targeted by Asset Invest.

turns.speaker: Marie Goldman
turns.text: In my Chelmsford constituency residents have been contacted by Asset Invest, which bought restrictive covenants in titles and is demanding tens of thousands of pounds when people try to sell.

turns.speaker: Marie Goldman
turns.text: People discover this when their property goes on Rightmove or when they're in probate; some feel pressured and have paid over £20,000 to avoid losing a sale.

turns.speaker: Dr Keiran Mullan
turns.text: At least 15 MPs have constituents affected; Asset Invest holds covenants in many more constituencies. Examples: one Gosport constituent paid £11,300, Stafford £7,500, and Fareham & Waterlooville over £10,000.

turns.speaker: Dr Keiran Mullan
turns.text: We met surveyors, lenders and solicitors and all agree it's a problem. A debate now would help set out the background before the Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill.

turns.speaker: Mary Glindon
turns.text: The Committee asks for an equal split of Government and Opposition speakers; your application names only one Government Back Bencher. Can you find three more?

turns.speaker: Dr Keiran Mullan
turns.text: Government MPs are often PPSs and hesitant to sign quickly. We can send a list of affected Government constituencies but the form asks for named supporters—so we'll approach them.

turns.speaker: Mr Dillon
turns.text: You said 15 MPs affected and then another 41 seats—does that mean about 56 constituencies in total?

turns.speaker: Dr Keiran Mullan
turns.text: At least. We've only tracked one housebuilder whose covenants were bought for £1, and we've since identified others, so the true number could be higher.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: How is Asset Invest identifying who benefits from covenants?

turns.speaker: Dr Keiran Mullan
turns.text: They've legally bought the covenant rights, so on paper they 'have the benefit'. They don't maintain or enforce standards—it's a revenue-seeking practice rather than a genuine planning or maintenance concern.

turns.speaker: Marie Goldman
turns.text: They seem to make the sums up and use pressure selling. Constituents pay because they'd rather lose money than risk a house sale collapsing.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: If you can supply four Government MPs who will actually speak in the debate (an even split of eight speakers), the Committee will support the application. Please send those names to the Clerks.

turns.speaker: Dr Keiran Mullan
turns.text: We'll approach the MPs and provide names. Thank you.

chapters.title: Protecting the next generation's freedom of religion or belief
chapters.takeaway: An MP requested a 90-minute Westminster Hall debate on protecting children’s freedom of religion or belief overseas, highlighting forced conversions and asking for FCDO engagement.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Next application: a debate on protecting the rights of the next generation to freedom of religion or belief. Jim, is this for a Tuesday Westminster Hall 90-minute slot?

turns.speaker: Jim Shannon
turns.text: Yes — I'm happy with Tuesday or Thursday. I'm chair of the APPG for international freedom of religion or belief. The focus is specifically on children and young people facing persecution, forced conversions and restrictions.

turns.speaker: Jim Shannon
turns.text: Freedom of religion or belief is a fundamental right (article 18 of the Universal Declaration and article 14 of the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child). Parliament has shown sustained cross-party interest.

turns.speaker: Jim Shannon
turns.text: We have had a special envoy and recent parliamentary scrutiny of forced conversions, especially in Pakistan, and I want time to put the next generation's needs on record and press for action.

turns.speaker: Mr Dillon
turns.text: Which Government Department should respond?

turns.speaker: Jim Shannon
turns.text: This is mainly an FCDO matter. I think Chris Elmore or Ministers covering the Far East would be appropriate given where forced conversions are being reported.

turns.speaker: Mr Dillon
turns.text: A practical point: your form was out of date and didn't ask which Department answers. The Clerks have sent you an updated form for future applications.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Davies
turns.text: I see Ruth Jones has been added to your backers, so the application now meets the Committee's composition rules.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thanks — the Clerks will be in touch to arrange the slot and ensure the right Department is invited. There's also a separate letter on Bangladesh moving through the office.

turns.speaker: Jim Shannon
turns.text: Thank you. I appreciate the Committee's help.

chapters.title: Debate to educate on harmful breeding of pets
chapters.takeaway: An MP sought an educational Westminster Hall debate to highlight the suffering caused by breeding cats and dogs for exaggerated features and the strain this places on rescues.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Ruth, please present your application on breeding dogs and cats with exaggerated features for a Westminster Hall debate.

turns.speaker: Ruth Jones
turns.text: This should be an educational debate. Breeding animals with flat faces, floppy ears or twisted tails causes pain, breathing problems and shortened lives, yet they're still promoted as cute.

turns.speaker: Ruth Jones
turns.text: Social media and celebrity culture encourage demand. People pester parents for these pets then discover they need expensive surgery—sometimes £6,000—so rescues are left to pick up the cost.

turns.speaker: Alison Hume
turns.text: There is a risk that emphasising suffering can encourage 'rescue' motivations rather than reducing demand. Is there any urgency about timing?

turns.speaker: Ruth Jones
turns.text: No specific timing. The goal is to raise public awareness so people think twice before buying and to reduce the pressure on rescue centres.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you. The Clerks will be in touch about arranging the debate and speakers.

turns.speaker: Ruth Jones
turns.text: Thanks very much.
